title: Tenali Raman and the Golden Bathhouse

full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, influenced by flatterers who urged him to rival the legendary opulence of Persian emperors, commissioned an extravagant private bathhouse in the palace.
The walls were lined with mirrors of polished silver, the tubs were carved from white marble inlaid with lapis lazuli, and the faucets were cast in solid gold.
The project cost fifty thousand gold dinars from the royal treasury.

The King invited his ministers to inspect the finished palace:
'Behold! Was there ever a bathhouse so divine in all the history of Bharatavarsha? Does it not elevate the majesty of the Emperor to bathe in pure gold?'

All the courtiers praised the extravagance with extravagant flattery.
Tenali Raman remained silent, observing the display.

The next morning, an extraordinary spectacle unfolded in the palace courtyard.
Tenali Raman arrived leading an ancient, mangy street donkey whose coat was caked in dried street mud and coal soot.
Tenali led the donkey straight into the new golden bathhouse!
He turned on the gold faucets, poured warm scented rosewater over the donkey’s back, lathered its fur with imported almond soap, and began rubbing the beast's ears with a silk towel!

The King, arriving for his morning bath, stood frozen in stunned outrage:
'Tenali! What unspeakable sacrilege is this? You are washing a filthy street donkey in the royal golden bathhouse?'

Tenali looked up with innocent sincerity:
'Maharaj, pardon my humble efforts! I noticed that this poor donkey was dirty, weary, and despised by all the horses in the city.
Remembering your royal words yesterday—that bathing in pure gold and scented rosewater elevates the majesty of the bather—I thought: "If gold can elevate a man into a glorious sovereign, surely an hour in this golden bath will transform this common donkey into a celestial white stallion!"'

The King stared at Tenali, then at the donkey, which was contentedly chewing on a garland of tuberoses.
Tenali added softly:
'Alas, Your Majesty! I have washed him for two hours, but he remains an ordinary donkey.
External gold cannot transform the nature of an animal, nor can extravagant marble baths add a single cubit to the true majesty of a monarch. While fifty thousand gold coins were spent on golden taps, three villages on our northern border lack clean drinking water wells.'

King Krishnadevaraya felt a deep pang of conscience. The biting truth of Tenali’s satire pierced through his vanity.
The King embraced Tenali:
'Thou hast opened my eyes, Tenali. A king’s true bath is the clean stream of justice.'
The King halted all further ostentatious construction, diverted royal funds to build irrigation tanks across the province, and gifted the donkey to an honest farmer with a supply of oats.
moral: A ruler’s true glory is not measured by ostentatious luxury, but by the clean prosperity of his humblest subjects.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Tenali and the Golden Bath"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
